params.question: Which biological feature of cervical carcinogenesis makes screening a uniquely powerful intervention compared to most other cancers?

answers.text: Cervical cancer is always preceded by visible genital warts caused by HPV, making clinical detection straightforward

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Genital warts are caused by low-risk HPV types (6 and 11), not the high-risk types (16 and 18) responsible for cervical cancer. Pre-invasive CIN lesions are invisible to the naked eye.

answers.text: All HPV-infected women develop invasive cancer within 5 years, so a single screening test at age 30 is sufficient

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Most HPV infections are cleared by the immune system. Only persistent high-risk HPV infections progress, and the timeline is 10 to 15 years — which is why repeated screening over a range of ages is recommended.

answers.text: The progression from HPV infection through CIN to invasive cancer spans 10 to 15 years, providing a wide window to detect and treat pre-invasive disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The stepwise progression (HPV → CIN 1 → CIN 2/3 → microinvasive → invasive cancer) over 10 to 15 years allows detection at the CIN 2/3 stage, where cryotherapy or LEEP achieves cure with minimal morbidity.

answers.text: Cervical cancer produces specific serum tumour markers detectable in routine blood investigations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no reliable serum tumour marker for early cervical cancer. Screening relies on cytology (Pap smear), VIA/VILI, HPV DNA testing, and colposcopy — not blood tests.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the natural history: HPV infection → CIN 1 → CIN 2/3 → microinvasive → invasive cancer. This stepwise progression over 10–15 years is what makes screening so effective — it catches disease at a curable stage.
Exactly right. The 10–15 year pre-invasive window is the reason cervical cancer is one of the few malignancies amenable to both primary (HPV vaccination) and secondary (screening) prevention.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old woman not on HRT presents with vaginal bleeding 10 years after men

params.question: A 62-year-old woman not on HRT presents with vaginal bleeding 10 years after menopause. The probability of endometrial cancer in postmenopausal women with PMB is approximately 10 to 15%. Despite most cases having a benign cause, why does this symptom mandate urgent investigation?

answers.text: Because postmenopausal bleeding is specific to endometrial cancer and excludes all benign causes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PMB is not specific to malignancy — atrophic vaginitis, cervical polyps, and endometrial polyps can all cause it. Its clinical importance lies in its sensitivity (present in ~90% of endometrial cancers), not its specificity.

answers.text: Because endometrial cancer detected at an early stage through PMB-prompted investigation is highly treatable, so the 10–15% probability justifies the clinical rule 'PMB is cancer until proven otherwise'

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Although benign causes account for the majority of PMB, the 10–15% probability of malignancy is clinically significant. Since early-stage endometrial cancer is curable, the rule ensures no treatable cancer is missed.

answers.text: Because transvaginal ultrasound alone can definitively diagnose endometrial cancer without the need for tissue sampling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transvaginal ultrasound is an important first-line investigation for measuring endometrial thickness, but histological confirmation via endometrial biopsy or curettage is required for definitive diagnosis.

answers.text: Because PMB always indicates Stage III disease requiring immediate hysterectomy without further workup

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PMB most often leads to diagnosis at an early stage (Stage I). Endometrial cancer presenting with PMB has a favourable prognosis precisely because the symptom is visible and alarming enough to prompt early presentation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key reasoning: ~90% of endometrial cancers present with PMB, the probability of cancer in a woman with PMB is 10–15%, and early-stage disease is highly curable. Together, these facts mandate investigation of every case of PMB.

Well analysed. The combination of a meaningful cancer probability (~10–15%), the high sensitivity of PMB (~90% of cases), and the curability of early-stage disease together justify treating PMB as cancer until proven otherwise.

params.question: A primigravida at 10 weeks presents with severe vomiting, a uterus palpable at 18 weeks' size, and serum β-hCG of 150,000 mIU/mL. Which analysis of the pathophysiology best explains the hyperemesis in this presentation?

answers.text: Hyperemesis is caused by mechanical pressure of a rapidly enlarging uterus on the stomach

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mechanical compression of the stomach occurs in late pregnancy, not at 10 weeks' gestation. The hyperemesis in molar pregnancy has a hormonal basis related to the markedly elevated β-hCG.

answers.text: Hyperemesis is a normal first-trimester symptom unrelated to the elevated β-hCG, and its severity here is coincidental

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While mild nausea is common in normal pregnancy, the severity of hyperemesis in molar pregnancy is directly proportional to the markedly elevated β-hCG levels, which are far above normal gestational values.

answers.text: The elevated β-hCG suppresses thyroid function, causing hypothyroidism that manifests as vomiting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The opposite is true. Markedly elevated β-hCG cross-reacts with TSH receptors to stimulate (not suppress) thyroid function, producing biochemical hyperthyroidism that contributes to hyperemesis.

answers.text: Markedly elevated β-hCG from trophoblastic proliferation cross-reacts with TSH receptors, stimulating thyroid activity and causing severe hyperemesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In a complete hydatidiform mole, abnormal trophoblastic proliferation produces markedly elevated β-hCG, which shares structural homology with TSH. This cross-reactivity stimulates thyroid hormone production, contributing to the severe hyperemesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a complete hydatidiform mole, abnormal trophoblastic tissue produces markedly elevated β-hCG. Because β-hCG shares structural homology with TSH, it cross-reacts with TSH receptors, stimulating thyroid activity and causing severe hyperemesis.

Excellent analysis. The β-hCG–TSH cross-reactivity is a key concept: it explains both the hyperemesis and the biochemical thyrotoxicosis seen in complete molar pregnancies with very high β-hCG levels.
